# Discussion

**Main finding.** On Gemma~3 270M, selected dual-effect interventions
produce large *total* effects on article--noun completions under free
generation, but noun-token changes are largely consistent with mediation
through the generated article (**H3**). When the article is held fixed and
interventions remain active, the tested sparse and dense handles give
little behaviorally sufficient control of same-article-class noun tokens,
especially when targets begin far below the decoding boundary.

**What we do and do not claim.** We do not claim that latent planning is
impossible, that @hanna2026latent's larger-model results are wrong, or
that an abstract \(C\to c\) edge is absent everywhere in the network. We
claim that free-generation metrics can overstate separable planning, that
\(b\) is a mediator rather than a classical confounder, and that the
tested handles do not function as independently editable noun-token
controls under fixed \(b\). Output package-like behavior does not by itself
identify a fused internal package representation (**H2**).

**Assay validation.** We screened near-boundary same-article-class pairs
and attempted oracle MLP-in activation patching under fixed native \(b\).
That construction did **not** produce clear noun-token control, so
fixed-\(b\) top-1 nulls cannot be read as a fully validated negative test
of every possible noun pathway. Continuous logit effects and uncertainty
intervals should be reported alongside top-1 rates whenever targets are
floor-limited.

**Methodological implication.** Before treating article-directed feature
interventions as modular planning evidence, hold the generated article
fixed, keep candidate interventions on, score noun-token logits (not only
switches), compare to matched random controls, and attempt a positive
control that can move noun tokens when such control exists.
